## Goals for today

::: {.nonincremental}
1. Learn about the use of **R packages**
2. Understand the **main object types** in R and their practical relevance
3. Learn how to **transform object types** into each other
4. Hear about some useful **helper functions** and the concept of **vectorisation**
:::

# Part I: Packages {.divider background-color="#EAF0F4"}

## R packages

- One good thing about R: a large community writes objects and functions that
  serve useful purposes and **makes them available to all**
- This is done via **R packages**

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
An R package = a collection of assignments and documentation that people pass
around
:::

- If you install R you can use all objects that you defined yourself, and all
  objects pre-defined in R
- To use objects defined by **someone else**, you must install their package

## Installing packages

- The official way to distribute packages is via **CRAN**, the *Comprehensive R
  Archive Network*
- To install a package deployed on CRAN:

::: {.small}
```r
install.packages("NAME OF PACKAGE")

install.packages("ineq")
```
:::

- For packages not yet released on CRAN, other functions are available
- After installing `ineq`, you can use all objects defined by it

## Calling objects defined in packages

- One object defined in `ineq` is the function `Gini()`
  - Simply calling `Gini()` does **not** work
- You must tell R that `Gini()` is defined by the package `ineq`, using `::`

::: {.small}
```r
ineq::Gini(c(1, 2, 3, 4))
```
:::

- Think of `::` as building a **bridge** between your session and the objects of
  a package
- A sometimes more convenient way is `library()` at the beginning of the script:

::: {.small}
```r
library(ineq)
```
:::

## Packages and masking

- Packages are written by many different people
- It is not unlikely that two packages assign the **same name** to different
  objects
- If you attach both, the assignment of the earlier package gets **masked**
  - Try it: attach `dplyr` and `plm`
  - In these cases you must use `::` to reach the masked object

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
Always use `::` whenever masking is a potential problem — it makes your code far
easier to understand, for you and for others
:::

::: {.smaller}
`conflicts()` shows all names for which conflicts exist
:::

## Recap questions {.divider background-color="#EAF0F4"}

::: {.nonincremental .smaller}
- What is the main rationale for the use of R packages?
- What is an R package in the most basic sense?
- How can you install R packages from CRAN? Illustrate this using `dplyr`
- How can you access objects from a package you installed previously? What are
  the advantages and disadvantages of the different ways?
- What does it mean to *attach* a package?
- What do we mean by *masking* in the context of using R packages?
:::

# Part II: Basic object types in R {.divider background-color="#EAF0F4"}

## Why types matter

::: {.pullquote}
To understand computations in R, two slogans are helpful:
Everything that exists is an **object**.
Everything that happens is a function call.
[John Chambers]{.source}
:::

- We have learned a lot about functions — now we turn to **objects**
- We must distinguish object types because **functions operate differently**
  depending on the type
  - 'Adding up' numbers is different from 'adding up' words
- Fortunately there are only a **few basic types**; the most general one is a
  **vector**

## The basic type hierarchy

::: {.mermaid-tight}
```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  O["Objects"] --> V["Vectors"]
  O --> N["NULL"]
  V --> A["Atomic vectors"]
  V --> L["Lists ('generic vectors')"]
  A --> lo["logical<br/><small>TRUE, FALSE</small>"]
  A --> in1["integer<br/><small>1, 2, 3, …</small>"]
  A --> db["double<br/><small>0.1, 1.0, 2.9, …</small>"]
  A --> ch["character<br/><small>'One', 'Hello', …</small>"]
  style A fill:#00395B,color:#ffffff,stroke:#00395B
  style L fill:#E2553C,color:#ffffff,stroke:#E2553C
  style V fill:#6E6E6E,color:#ffffff,stroke:#6E6E6E
  style O fill:#D9D9D9,color:#333333,stroke:#D9D9D9
  style N fill:#D9D9D9,color:#333333,stroke:#D9D9D9
```
:::

::: {.smaller}
Among the more specific vector types we will meet **factors** and **data frames**
later
:::

## Atomic vectors

- Atomic vectors are composed **only of objects of the same type**
  - An atomic vector is of the same type as its elements
  - Test it with `typeof()`

::: {.columns .smaller}
::: {.column width="25%"}
**`logical`**

Only two options: `TRUE` or `FALSE` — often the result of logical operations
(e.g. `4 > 2`)
:::

::: {.column width="25%"}
**`integer`**

A whole number followed by `L`: `1L`, `2L`, `100L` — often the result of counting
:::

::: {.column width="25%"}
**`double`**

A number with a decimal sign: `2.0`, `0.8`, `-7.5` — the 'standard' number you
will use
:::

::: {.column width="25%"}
**`character`**

All kinds of tokens, starting and ending with `"`: `"2"`, `"Hello!"`, `"vec_1"`
:::
:::

::: {.tiny .muted}
Missing values are also considered logical in some instances — basically
irrelevant for now
:::

## Creating atomic vectors

- The easiest way is the function `c()` ('concatenate'):

::: {.small}
```r
t_vec <- c(1, 2, 3)
```
:::

- The number of elements in a vector is its **length**, tested with `length()`:

::: {.small}
```r
length(t_vec)
```
:::

- `c()` can also **merge** atomic vectors of arbitrary length:

::: {.small}
```r
t_vec_2  <- c(4, 5, 6)
t_vec_full <- c(t_vec, t_vec_2)
```
:::

## Coercion

- Sometimes we want to **change the type** of an atomic vector
- The functions `as.*()` and `is.*()` are useful — substitute `*` by the type:

::: {.small}
```r
xx <- "2"
is.double(xx)
yy <- as.double(xx)
is.double(yy)
```
:::

- But beware of counter-intuitive transformation behaviour:

::: {.small}
```r
as.integer(22.9)
as.logical(99)
```
:::

## Intermediate exercises {.divider background-color="#EAF0F4"}

::: {.nonincremental}
1. Create a vector containing the numbers `2`, `5`, `2.4` and `11`
2. What is the **type** of this vector?
3. Transform this vector into the type `integer`. What happens?
4. Do you think you can create a vector containing `"2"`, `"Hallo"`, `4.0` and
   `TRUE`? Why, or why not?
:::

# Part III: Helper functions, indexing, vectorisation {.divider background-color="#EAF0F4"}

## Sequences: `seq()`

Some vector types you create frequently: sequences, concatenated words,
repetitions

For sequences, use `seq()`:

::: {.smaller}
- `from`, `to` — starting and end values of the sequence
- `by` — increment steps (must be numeric)
- `length.out` — desired length of the final sequence
- `along.with` — creates a sequence of the same length as an object
:::

Only **one** of `by`, `length.out`, `along.with` can be used:

::: {.small}
```r
seq(-5, 5, by = 2.5)
seq(1, 4, length.out = 10)
```
:::

## Pasting and repeating

For concatenated words, use `paste()` with the argument `sep`:

::: {.small}
```r
paste("file_", seq(1, 4), ".pdf", sep = "")
```
:::

::: {.smaller}
`sep` specifies how the input vectors should be separated
:::

For repetitions, use `rep()`:

::: {.small}
```r
rep("Cool!", 5)
```
:::

## Indexing

- Indexing means **referencing a particular position** of a vector
- You do this by adding the position in square brackets:

::: {.small}
```r
v_c <- c("First", "Second", "Second", "Fourth")
v_c[3]              # returns the third element
v_c[3] <- "Third!"  # replaces it
```
:::

- But you **cannot** use this to add new elements beyond the current length in
  an arbitrary way:

::: {.small}
```r
v_c[5] <- "Fifth…"
```
:::

- Add a fifth element to `v_c`!

## Vectorisation

- One reason atomic vectors are so popular: they allow for **very fast
  computations**
  - For the computer it is much easier to work with sets of objects that all
    behave the same
- **Vectorisation** means an operation is applied to *each element* of a vector:

::: {.small}
```r
v_2 <- seq(1, 5)
v_2**2
```
:::

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
'To vectorise' a task means writing it so operations apply to atomic vectors —
in R you should do that whenever possible
:::

::: {.smaller}
The slower alternative are **loops**, which we learn about later and which are
unavoidable in certain situations
:::

::: {.nonincremental}
1. Create a vector with the numbers from `-2` to `19`, step size `0.75`
2. Create an **index vector** for this vector (a vector with all possible indices
   of the original vector)
3. Compute the **log** of each element using vectorisation. Anything that draws

:::

::: {.smaller}
Remember: check the type of an atomic vector with `typeof()`
:::

# Part IV: Lists {.divider background-color="#EAF0F4"}

## Lists

- The **second major type of vectors** → sometimes called *generic vectors*
- Difference to atomic vectors: lists may contain **objects of different types**

::: {.small}
```r
l_1 <- list(c(1, 2), c("a", "b"), c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE))
typeof(l_1)
```
:::

- Lists can be complex → get an overview using `str()`:

::: {.small}
```r
> str(l_1)
List of 3
 $ : num  [1:2] 1 2
 $ : chr  [1:2] "a" "b"
 $ : logi [1:3] TRUE FALSE FALSE
```
:::

::: {.smaller}
`List of 3` = number of elements · `num`/`chr`/`logi` = types · `[1:2]` = lengths
· the rest = a preview
:::

## Naming and indexing of lists

- The elements of lists can be **named**:

::: {.small}
```r
l_2 <- list("numbers" = c(1, 2),
            "letters" = c("a", "b"),
            "logics"  = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE))
```
:::

- Retrieve the names with `names(l_2)`
- **Subset** the list using the names → returns a *list*:

::: {.small}
```r
l_2["letters"]
```
:::

- **Access the elements** of the sublists with `[[` → returns the *content*:

::: {.small}
```r
l_2[["letters"]]
l_2$letters        # shortcut
```
:::

## Practical differences to atomic vectors

Two very important differences:

- **Vectorisation does not work** for lists
- **Indexing works differently** for lists

::: {.columns .small}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```r
v_ <- c(1, 2, 3); 2 * v_
l_ <- list(1, 2, 3); 2 * l_
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```r
typeof(l_[1])
typeof(l_[[1]])
```
:::
:::

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
Lists are fundamental to the more complex data structures we will encounter
later — including data frames
:::

## `NA` — absent elements

- `NA` represents **absent elements** of vectors
  - Happens frequently when vectors contain observations
  - Many functions behave differently when `NA`s are present — remember `na.rm`:

::: {.small}
```r
mean(c(1, 2, NA))
mean(c(1, 2, NA), na.rm = TRUE)
```
:::

- Test for `NA` with `is.na()`, check a whole vector with `anyNA()`:

::: {.small}
```r
is.na(c(1, 2, NA))
anyNA(c(1, 2, NA))
```
:::

## `NULL` — the absent vector

- `NULL` is a data type in itself, but in practice best thought of as a
  **vector of length zero**:

::: {.small}
```r
c()
typeof(NULL)
length(NULL)
is.null(NULL)
```
:::

- You use `NULL` mainly in two situations:
  - Represent an **empty vector** of arbitrary type
  - Represent an **absent vector** — as opposed to `NA`, which represents absent
    *elements* of a vector

- Create a list with three **named** elements: `"A"`, `"B"` and `"C"`
- `"A"` should contain the **square root** of the numbers from `-2` to `8`
  (step size `1`)
- `"B"` should contain the **log** of the numbers between `2` and `4`
  (step size `0.5`)
- `"C"` should contain letters from `a1` to `g7`

::: {.smaller}
Hint for C: use the pre-defined vector `letters` and the function `paste()`
:::

## Wrap up

::: {.nonincremental}
The central take-aways concern:

- How to **test for and transform** these types: `typeof()`, `is.*()`, `as.*()`
- How to **index** them: `[`, `[[`, `$`
- How to **create typical instances**: `rep()`, `paste()`, `seq()`
:::

- We learned about **vectorisation** and its attractiveness in R
- We encountered the 'strange' types `NA`, `NULL` and `NaN`
